title: AI Implementation Roadmap
summary: A phased 90-day roadmap for rolling out AI from a bounded pilot to a trained team, with owners, guardrails, and success measures at each stage.
audience: Leaders and operators planning a controlled first 90 days of AI adoption.
assumptions: The first pilot is bounded and reversible
limitations: A generic 90-day plan must be adapted to organizational and regulatory context
Milestones do not guarantee successful adoption
editorialIntro: A rollout you can trust doesn't start with a tool. It starts with one use case, a data rule, and a person who owns it. This 90-day template moves you from first pilot to trained team in four phases, each with a goal, an owner, guardrails, and a way to tell if it worked.

blocks.text: A four-phase, roughly 90-day plan for putting AI to work without the two failure modes we see most: buying a tool nobody adopts, or moving so fast that one sensitive-data mistake ends the whole effort. Each phase carries a single goal, a named owner, the guardrails that keep it safe, and a success measure — so you know whether to keep going or fix something first.
It picks up where the AI Use Case Inventory leaves off. Once you've ranked your opportunities, this is how you turn the top one into a real, adopted change — then a second, then a third.

items: Owners and operators who've decided to try AI and want a sequence to follow instead of a pile of open tabs.
Department leads asked to "roll out AI" who need a plan they can defend to their team and their boss.
Anyone who ran one good AI experiment and now has to spread it without losing the quality or the trust.
Four phases — Foundation, Pilot, Expand, Embed — mapped across 13 weeks, each with a goal, key activities, an owner, guardrails, and a success measure.
A copy-pastable fill-in version of the whole roadmap, with target-date fields for every phase.
A short "before you start" checklist and a review-cadence note so the plan doesn't stall after week two.
A guardrail reminder about the two corners you should never cut to move faster.
Pick one use case. Take the top low-effort, low-sensitivity row from your inventory. One. Resist the urge to run three at once.
Assign an owner per phase. Every phase needs one name accountable for it, not a committee. Owners can differ by phase.
Set the guardrails before the work. Decide your data-handling rule and your human-review step in Phase 0, before anyone touches a tool.
Move on measures, not vibes. Each phase has a success measure. Hit it before advancing; if you miss it, fix the phase you're in.
Fill the dates and review weekly. Put real target dates on each phase and hold a short weekly check-in to keep it honest.

blocks.text: Here's the full phased plan with realistic content in each cell. Treat the specifics as a worked example — a small services business rolling out AI-assisted customer replies — and swap in your own use case, names, and dates. Then copy the fill-in version below and work it phase by phase.

AI IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP — 90 DAYS USE CASE (one, from your inventory): ______________________________ OVERALL OWNER: ______________________________ START DATE: ______________________________ BEFORE YOU START — CHECKLIST [ ] We picked ONE use case, not several. [ ] We wrote one plain-language data-handling rule. [ ] We chose a tool tier (consumer / business / private) that fits the data. [ ] Every phase has a named owner (a person, not a committee). [ ] We agreed on one example of a "good" AI output. [ ] Leadership knows this is happening and supports it. ------------------------------------------------------------------ PHASE 0 · FOUNDATION (Weeks 1-2) Goal: Pick one use case and set the rules before any real use. Activities: - Pick one use case from the inventory: ____________________ - Write the data rule: ____________________ - Choose the tool tier: ____________________ - Agree what "good" looks like: ____________________ - Name the pilot owner + 1-2 users: ____________________ Owner: ____________________ Guardrails: Data rule + tool tier written and shared BEFORE Phase 1. Success measure: One-page scope the team has read and agreed to. Target date: ____________________ ------------------------------------------------------------------ PHASE 1 · PILOT (Weeks 3-5) Goal: Prove the use case works safely with 1-2 people + human review. Activities: - Run the task on real work following Phase 0 rules - Require human review on every output - Build a small prompt / example set - Log wins, misses, near-misses on data - Track time saved vs. baseline Owner: ____________________ Guardrails: 100% human review. No expansion until success measure met. Success measure: 20+ real tasks, clear time saving, zero data-rule breaches. Target date: ____________________ ------------------------------------------------------------------ PHASE 2 · EXPAND (Weeks 6-9) Goal: Roll out to a small group; optionally add a second use case. Activities: - Extend to 4-8 people (NOT the whole company) - Write a short "how we do this" guide - Run a 60-minute training session - Optionally start a 2nd use case at Phase 1 discipline - Loosen review only where proven safe; document where Owner: ____________________ Guardrails: Same data rule for all. New users keep full review until they hit the quality bar. Small group only. Success measure: Group uses it independently; quality holds; time saved scales. Target date: ____________________ ------------------------------------------------------------------ PHASE 3 · EMBED (Weeks 10-13) Goal: Make it a normal, owned part of how the team works. Activities: - Fold the guide + data rule into onboarding - Assign a standing process owner - Set a monthly quality + data-handling check - Pick the next use case (back to Phase 0) - Capture total quarterly time saved Owner: ____________________ Guardrails: Written policy, documented review standard, monthly audit. Success measure: Runs without the pilot team; named owner; next use case queued. Target date: ____________________ ------------------------------------------------------------------ REVIEW CADENCE Weekly (15 min): Are we on the target date? Any data near-misses? Blockers? End of each phase: Did we hit the success measure? Yes = advance. No = fix here first. Monthly (from Phase 3 on): Quality, data handling, tool tier still right?

Don't cut these corners to move faster: skipping the Phase 0 guardrails — the written data rule and the human-review step — is how a rollout turns into a data leak or a customer-facing mistake. And don't jump from a two-person pilot straight to the whole company; expand to a small group, prove quality holds, then widen. This is general education, not legal advice — check your own obligations before you move any sensitive data or set company policy.

title: AI Policy Starter Kit
summary: A plain-language internal AI-use policy template covering approved and prohibited uses, human review, confidentiality, and audit controls.
audience: Small teams preparing a first internal AI policy for qualified review.
methodology: Adapt every clause to real practice
assumptions: The template will be adapted and reviewed
The organization will train and enforce the resulting policy
limitations: The template is educational and is not legal advice
It cannot account for every jurisdiction, contract, or regulated use
editorialIntro: A plain-English internal AI-use policy your team will actually read and follow. It's a starting draft — adapt it to how your business really works, then have qualified counsel review it before you adopt it. It isn't legal advice, and it isn't finished until you've made it yours.

blocks.text: A short, usable internal policy that tells your team where AI helps, where it doesn't belong, and who owns what comes out of it. It's written to be read: plain language, sensible defaults, no wall of boilerplate. You fill in the bracketed placeholders, cut the parts that don't fit, and end up with something people follow instead of a document that lives in a drawer.
The whole thing runs about one to two pages once you've adapted it. That's on purpose. A policy people finish reading beats a perfect one nobody opens.

items: Owners and operators who want AI used across the business without a data leak or a decision made on autopilot.
Managers who keep getting asked "am I allowed to use AI for this?" and want a clear answer to point to.
Small teams with no legal or compliance department who still need something written down before staff start pasting work into chatbots.
A ten-section policy covering purpose, approved and prohibited uses, tools, confidentiality, human review, disclosure, security, audit, and sign-off.
Real starter language — sentences you could adopt after review, not headings you fill in from scratch.
Bracketed placeholders for your company name, roles, tools, contacts, and review dates.
A standing rule baked throughout: a named human owns and verifies every AI-assisted output.
Copy it out. Use the Copy button on the template below and drop it into a doc.
Fill the placeholders. Swap every [bracketed] item for your real company name, roles, tools, and contacts.
Cut and adapt. Delete sections that don't apply, tighten the ones that do, and add anything specific to your industry or contracts.
Circulate for feedback. Share the draft with the people who'll live under it and fix what doesn't match reality.
Have it reviewed. Get qualified counsel — an attorney and, where relevant, a security or compliance advisor — to review it before you adopt.
Set a review date and get sign-off. Put a date on the calendar to revisit it, and have each person acknowledge it.

blocks.text: Template for review — not legal advice. This is a starting draft. Adapt it to your business and have qualified counsel review it before you adopt it. Your obligations depend on your industry, your contracts, and your local laws. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney, and nothing here is legal advice.
Here's the draft. It's written to be readable and genuinely adoptable after review. Copy it, make it yours, and don't skip the review step.

[COMPANY NAME] — INTERNAL AI-USE POLICY Version [1.0] · Effective [DATE] · Next review [DATE] · Owner: [ROLE/NAME] TEMPLATE FOR REVIEW — This is a starting draft, not legal advice. Adapt it to your business and have a qualified professional review it before you adopt it. 1. PURPOSE & SCOPE This policy explains how we use AI tools at [COMPANY NAME] so we get the benefits without putting our clients, our data, or our reputation at risk. It applies to everyone who does work for us — employees, contractors, and anyone acting on our behalf. "AI tools" means any software that generates or analyzes content using machine learning or large language models — chat assistants, writing and image tools, coding assistants, transcription and summarization services, and similar tools, whether standalone or built into apps we already use. The rule underneath everything here: AI helps you work; it does not do the work for you. A person is always responsible for what goes out. 2. APPROVED USES You're encouraged to use approved AI tools to work faster and better. Good uses include: - Drafting first versions of emails, documents, and posts (you edit and own it) - Summarizing long documents, threads, meetings, or notes - Brainstorming ideas, angles, names, and outlines - Research starting points — to orient yourself, not to cite as fact - Code assistance — suggestions, explanations, and boilerplate The standing rule for all of these: a human owns and verifies every output. Whatever the tool produces, you read it, check it, correct it, and take responsibility for it before it goes anywhere. 3. PROHIBITED USES Do not: - Enter confidential, client, or personal data into any tool that isn't on our approved list (see Section 4). - Treat AI output as final legal, medical, or financial advice. It's a draft or a starting point; qualified people make those calls. - Present AI-generated text or media as human-created where honesty requires disclosure (see Section 7). - Use AI to make high-stakes decisions about people — hiring, firing, discipline, credit, benefits — without real human judgment reviewing the decision. - Bypass security controls, licensing terms, or another tool's usage rules to get an AI feature, or feed it content we don't have the right to use. When you're unsure whether something is prohibited, stop and ask [ROLE/CONTACT] before you do it. 4. APPROVED TOOLS & TIERS Only use tools on this list for work, at the tier and for the data noted. Keep this list current; [ROLE] maintains it. TOOL | APPROVED TIER | DATA ALLOWED --------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------- [Tool name] | [e.g. Enterprise/Team] | [e.g. internal, no client PII] [Tool name] | [e.g. Business] | [e.g. public info only] [Tool name] | [Free/consumer] | [Non-sensitive only] If a tool isn't listed, it isn't approved for company data. Ask [ROLE] to review it before you use it for work. 5. CONFIDENTIALITY & DATA HANDLING Never put the following into consumer or free-tier AI tools: - Client or customer personal information (PII) - Passwords, keys, or credentials - Trade secrets or unreleased plans - Regulated data (health, financial, or anything under a contract or law) For anything sensitive, use only an approved enterprise tier that we've vetted for data handling ([TIER/TOOL PLACEHOLDER]). When in doubt about whether data is safe to enter, don't — ask [ROLE] first. Describing a task in the abstract is usually enough; you rarely need to paste the real records. 6. HUMAN REVIEW & ACCOUNTABILITY Every AI-assisted output has a named human who is accountable for it — normally the person who created or requested it. That person verifies the work before it's used or shared: check facts, figures, quotes, code, and anything the tool might have invented. Higher stakes mean stronger review. A rough internal summary needs a quick read. Anything that goes to a client, the public, a regulator, or into a system of record needs careful checking, and for the highest-stakes work, a second set of eyes. Nothing external goes out on a tool's word alone. 7. DISCLOSURE & TRANSPARENCY Be honest about AI assistance where it matters. Disclose when: - A client, partner, or regulation requires it. - Someone would reasonably feel misled to learn AI wrote or heavily shaped it — for example, a personal message, a testimonial, or professional advice. - You're using AI in a context (like certain filings or submissions) where the rules require a human author or a disclosure. Routine drafting help you've fully edited and taken ownership of generally doesn't need a disclosure. If you're unsure, disclose or ask [ROLE]. 8. SECURITY - Use your own company-provisioned accounts. Don't share logins or let others use your AI access. - Follow our normal access and password rules; use approved sign-in methods. - Don't install unvetted AI browser extensions or plugins on work devices. - Report any suspected data exposure, account compromise, or misuse to [CONTACT/EMAIL] as soon as you notice it. Fast reporting limits harm and won't get you in trouble. 9. AUDIT & RECORD-KEEPING Keep a lightweight log of high-stakes AI-assisted work — what the work was, which tool, and who reviewed it. It doesn't need to be heavy; a simple shared list is fine. This helps us learn what's working and answer questions if they come up. [ROLE] reviews the approved tool list and this policy at least [quarterly/annually] and updates them as tools and rules change. Next scheduled review: [DATE]. 10. ACKNOWLEDGMENT I have read and understand [COMPANY NAME]'s Internal AI-Use Policy and agree to follow it. Name: ______________________________ Role: ____________________ Signature: _________________________ Date: ____________________

One more time, because it matters: this is a template for review, not legal advice. It's a sensible starting draft, but your obligations depend on your industry, your contracts, and your local laws. Adapt it, then have qualified counsel review it before you adopt it. RN Collins is a JD candidate, not a licensed attorney, and nothing here is legal advice.

title: AI Tool Evaluation Matrix
summary: A weighted matrix for comparing AI tools across capability, security, cost, usability, integration, and support so decisions rest on evidence rather than hype.
audience: Teams comparing AI products for a defined workflow.
methodology: Distinguish documented claims from observed performance
Require qualified security and legal review where needed
assumptions: The workflow and acceptance criteria are defined
Time-sensitive vendor information is independently verified
limitations: Scores depend on chosen weights and evidence quality
Products, pricing, policies, and model routing change
editorialIntro: Every AI vendor sounds great in a demo. This matrix makes you compare them the boring way — on weighted criteria you set before you look at a single product — so the tool you pick wins on evidence, not on whoever gave the smoothest pitch.

blocks.text: A weighted scoring matrix for choosing between AI tools. You decide which criteria matter and how much each one counts, score every tool on your shortlist against the same scale, and let the weighted math surface a ranked answer. It doesn't replace judgment — it makes your judgment explicit, so a decision you can defend replaces a gut call you can't.
It works on a whiteboard, in a spreadsheet, or in the plain-text version below. What matters is that everyone scores against the same criteria with the same key, before anyone falls for a logo.

items: Owners and operators picking between two or three AI tools, tired of feature lists that all read the same.
Department leads who have to justify a purchase to finance, IT, or a skeptical boss with something better than "it felt right."
Anyone running a procurement or pilot who has to show their work — why this tool, on what basis, over the alternatives.
A weighted criteria table with sensible starting weights across capability, security, accuracy, ease of use, cost, integration, and support.
A fully worked example scoring three tools, with the arithmetic shown so you can watch weighting change the outcome.
A blank, copy-pastable matrix that drops into a spreadsheet, with a scoring key, the weighted-score formula, and a decision rule.
A hard rule on security: a tool that fails a data-security or compliance check is out, no matter how high it scores elsewhere.
Set criteria and weights first. Before you look at a single tool, agree on what matters and how much. Starting weights are below; adjust them to your business. Weights must sum to 100%.
Define what "good" looks like. For each criterion, write a plain sentence describing a 5. That is what stops scoring from turning into a popularity contest.
Score each tool 1–5. Same scale, same reviewers, same evidence. Score from a real trial where you can, not from the sales deck.
Multiply and total. Weighted score = raw score × weight. Add the weighted scores per tool. Highest total leads.
Apply the hard fail. Cross off any tool that can't meet your data-security or compliance bar, even if it "won" on points. Then pilot the leader before you sign.

blocks.text: 1 · Weighted criteria

These weights are a defensible starting point for most small and mid-sized businesses. Move them to match your reality — a regulated firm might push security to 30%; a solo operator might weight ease of use higher. Just keep the column summing to 100.

cells.text: Capability / fit for your use case
Does the actual job you need, well, on your real inputs — not just an adjacent demo task.
Clear data handling, no training on your data by default, meets your compliance needs, and can prove it.
Consistent, correct output you can trust; errors are rare, visible, and easy to catch.
Your team can learn it fast and will actually use it, not abandon it after week one.
Fair price including setup, training, seats, and overage — not just the sticker on the pricing page.
Connects to the tools you already run without a custom project or brittle workarounds.
Responsive support, a credible company, and a roadmap heading where you need it to.

blocks.text: 2 · Worked example

Here is the matrix filled in for three imaginary tools so you can watch the weighting do its work. These are placeholders — Tool A, B, and C — not real products, and the scores are made up to show the arithmetic. Each cell shows the raw score (1–5) and, in parentheses, the weighted score: raw × weight (as a decimal). Capability weighted 25% with a raw 5 gives 5 × 0.25 = 1.25.

Read what the weighting reveals. Tool C scored a perfect 5 on ease of use and cost — the things that feel good in a demo — but its low security score (2) dragged it to last, because security carries real weight. Tool A and Tool B finish neck and neck (4.00 vs 3.95): A leads on raw capability, B leads on security. That is the moment to stop and think, not to trust the second decimal. And note this next part carefully: if your security bar is non-negotiable and Tool C can't clear it, C is disqualified before totals even matter — the 3.30 is irrelevant. Points break ties among tools that pass the gate. They don't let a tool buy its way past a hard fail.
3 · Copy the blank matrix
Paste this into a spreadsheet (it splits on the pipe |, or retype it as columns) and score your own shortlist. Fill the weighted cells with raw × weight, then total each tool's column.

AI TOOL EVALUATION MATRIX SCORING KEY (raw score, per criterion, per tool) 1 = poor does not meet the need 2 = weak meets it partially, with real gaps 3 = adequate gets the job done, nothing special 4 = strong clearly good, minor gaps 5 = excellent best-in-class for your use case FORMULA Weighted score = raw score (1-5) x weight (as a decimal) Example: raw 4 on a 20% criterion = 4 x 0.20 = 0.80 Tool total = sum of that tool's weighted scores (out of a possible 5.00) Criterion | Weight | Tool A (raw / wtd) | Tool B (raw / wtd) | Tool C (raw / wtd) Capability / fit for use case | 0.25 | / | / | / Data security & privacy | 0.20 | / | / | / Accuracy / reliability | 0.15 | / | / | / Ease of use & adoption | 0.15 | / | / | / Cost / total cost of ownership | 0.10 | / | / | / Integration with your stack | 0.10 | / | / | / Vendor support & roadmap | 0.05 | / | / | / WEIGHTED TOTAL (out of 5.00) | 1.00 | | | DECISION NOTE Highest weighted total wins -- BUT any hard fail on data security or compliance is disqualifying, regardless of the total. A tool that cannot meet your security bar is out before totals matter. When totals are close (within ~0.15), don't trust the decimal -- run a short real pilot to break the tie. Weights must sum to 1.00 (100%).

Before you commit: a tool that fails your data-security or compliance requirements is disqualified regardless of its total score — points can't buy a tool past a hard fail. Verify vendor security claims yourself; "we're SOC 2" on a slide is not proof, so ask for the report and read your own contract terms. And run a real, short pilot on your actual work before you sign — a demo shows the tool at its best, a pilot shows it at yours. This is general education, not legal advice — check your own regulatory and contractual obligations before moving any data.

title: AI Use Case Inventory
summary: A worksheet for cataloging where AI could help a business and ranking candidates by value, effort, evidence, consequence, and readiness.
audience: Organizations beginning an AI opportunity and risk inventory.
assumptions: Workflow owners provide materially accurate information
Scores are reviewed rather than treated as automatic decisions
limitations: An inventory is not a technical or legal feasibility assessment
Incomplete workflow evidence can distort rankings
editorialIntro: Most teams buy the tool before they name the problem. This worksheet reverses that: list every place AI might help, score each for value and effort, and let the ranking decide where your first month goes.

blocks.text: A one-page inventory you fill in with your team. You write down the tasks across your business, ballpark the hours each one eats, note what AI could realistically do, and score every idea. The arithmetic does the prioritizing, so your first month lands on work that pays back fastest instead of the flashiest demo.
No special software required. A whiteboard, a spreadsheet, or the plain-text version below all work. The thinking is the deliverable, not the format.

items: Owners deciding where AI fits before spending a dollar on tools or consultants.
Department leads who keep fielding "can't we just use AI for this?" and want a defensible answer.
Anyone running a pilot who has to explain why this use case went first.
A worked example with real rows across support, marketing, operations, sales, finance, and HR.
A blank, copy-pastable version that drops straight into a spreadsheet or doc.
A scoring key so everyone in the room grades the same way.
A note on what data to keep out of consumer AI tools while you work.
Brain-dump first. Go department by department. List every repetitive, rule-following, or writing-heavy task. Capture, don't judge.
Estimate the time. Ballpark hours per week for each row. Rough is fine — you're ranking, not billing.
Name what AI could do. Be specific: "draft the first version," "summarize the thread," "flag the outliers." If you can't name the job, it isn't ready.
Score value and effort. Use the key below. Value is how much a win matters; effort is how hard it is to set up and trust.
Sort by priority. Priority = Value minus Effort. Start at the top, with low-sensitivity items, and prove one win before you spread out.

blocks.text: Here is a filled example so you can see the shape of good rows. Yours will differ — this is a sample business, not a recommendation.

cells.text: Draft from order status + past tickets
One blog post into social + email
Draft platform versions from the source
Compile public info into a brief

blocks.text: Rows 1 and 2 rise to the top: high value, low effort, low sensitivity. That is where you start. Row 8 is valuable but hard and touches sensitive data — a later project, not a first pilot.
Copy the blank worksheet
Paste this into a spreadsheet (it splits on the pipe |) or a doc, and start filling rows.

# | Department | Task/Process | Frequency | Time now (hrs/wk) | AI could... | Value (1-5) | Effort (1-5) | Priority (V-E) | Data sensitivity | Notes 1 | | | | | | | | | | 2 | | | | | | | | | | 3 | | | | | | | | | | 4 | | | | | | | | | | 5 | | | | | | | | | | 6 | | | | | | | | | | 7 | | | | | | | | | | 8 | | | | | | | | | | SCORING KEY Value (1-5): How much does a win here matter? 1 = minor convenience 3 = saves real time or cuts errors 5 = moves revenue, cost, or customer experience Effort (1-5): How hard to set up and trust? 1 = one prompt, use today 3 = needs setup, examples, or review 5 = new system, integration, or heavy oversight Priority = Value - Effort. Sort high to low. Start with high-priority, LOW data-sensitivity items. Prove one win, then expand.

Before you fill this in: don't paste confidential data, client PII, financials, or anything under contract into consumer AI tools while you inventory. Describe the task in the abstract. If a use case only works by feeding it sensitive data, mark it "High" and handle it with a private or approved tool later. This is general education, not legal advice — check your own obligations before moving sensitive data anywhere.

title: AI Workflow Mapping Worksheet
summary: Map a recurring workflow step by step, then identify where AI can assist, where humans retain authority, and where risk and evidence requirements live.
audience: Operators, consultants, and teams documenting workflows before introducing AI.
assumptions: People who perform the work participate
The map is validated against real examples
limitations: A diagram can omit tacit work and informal exceptions
Workflow suitability does not establish security, privacy, or compliance
editorialIntro: Pick one workflow you run over and over. Break it into steps. Then mark exactly where AI can help, where a human has to stay in the loop, and where the real risk lives before anything goes out the door.

blocks.text: Most "should we use AI here?" conversations stall because nobody has written down what the work actually is. This worksheet fixes that. You take a single recurring process, lay it out step by step, and label each step with one honest decision: does AI draft it, assist with it, run it on its own, or should a person do it and only a person?

The point is not to hand the whole thing to a model. The point is to find the two or three steps where AI genuinely saves time, keep a named human on the steps that carry risk, and be able to explain both to anyone who asks.

items: Owners and operators who keep hearing "we should use AI for that" but have not decided which part of "that" is safe to automate.
Team leads who want to hand a repeatable process to their people with clear guardrails instead of a vague "use ChatGPT."
Anyone whose workflow touches customer data, money, or promises, and who needs to prove a person still checks the output.
A worked example: one common workflow mapped end to end, so you can see what a finished map looks like.
A blank, copy-and-paste worksheet you can fill in for any process you run.
A short legend of four AI roles so you and your team use the same words for the same thing.
Name one workflow you do at least weekly. Write down what starts it and what "done" looks like.
List every step as it happens today, before any AI. Be honest about the messy ones.
For each step, pick one AI role: Draft, Assist, Automate, or Human-only. When in doubt, pick the more cautious one.
For every step that touches customer data or makes a promise, write down who verifies what before it leaves.
Note the risk if that step goes wrong, and how sensitive the data is. That tells you where to slow down.

blocks.text: Here is one everyday workflow mapped all the way through — responding to an inbound customer email. Notice that AI does real work in the middle, but a person owns every step that reaches the customer.

cells.text: Message lands in the shared inbox; someone eyeballs it.
Rep reads the actual message, not just the AI summary.
Miss an urgent or angry customer.
Rep decides: billing, support, sales, or spam.
Spot-check tags weekly; low stakes if a tag is wrong.
Rep looks up the customer's order or account history.
Rep confirms it's the right account before trusting it.
Rep writes a response from scratch.
Rep rewrites anything that sounds off or over-promises.
Wrong facts, wrong tone in your name.
Rep confirms dates, prices, refund amounts, policy.
Named rep verifies every number and commitment.
Promise you can't keep; wrong refund.
Rep is the one who sends; AI never sends on its own.
Rep notes the outcome and sets a reminder if needed.
Review the log during weekly inbox review.

blocks.text: Copy the blank worksheet
Copy the text below into a doc and fill it in for one of your own workflows. It has a header block and five blank step blocks. Add more step blocks if your workflow needs them.

AI WORKFLOW MAPPING WORKSHEET ============================= WORKFLOW NAME: ____________________________________________ OWNER (who runs it): ______________________________________ TRIGGER (what starts it): _________________________________ "DONE" MEANS: _____________________________________________ AI ROLE LEGEND -------------- Draft = AI produces a first version; a person edits before use. Assist = AI helps a person do the step (summarize, look up, suggest). Automate = AI runs the step on its own. ONLY for low-risk, reversible steps. Human-only = A person does this. No AI. Read this before you automate anything: every step that touches customer data or makes a promise on your behalf needs a named human checkpoint — a specific person who verifies a specific thing — before it goes out. title: Content Repurposing Workflow
summary: A repeatable workflow and prompt set for turning one strong source into a newsletter, social posts, short video scripts, and other channel-ready assets.
audience: Creators, founders, experts, and lean marketing teams repurposing source-grounded content.
methodology: Draft for one channel at a time
assumptions: The source is accurate and authorized for reuse
A human editor checks every derivative
limitations: The workflow cannot establish rights to third-party material
Condensation can remove nuance even when facts remain accurate
editorialIntro: You already made the hard thing — a blog post, a talk, a webinar. This workflow turns that one pillar into a week of assets across email, LinkedIn, video, and more, using a repeatable map and six copy-paste prompts. You still write the voice; the draft just starts faster.

blocks.text: A two-part template. The first part is a map: one pillar asset in, a set of derivative assets out, with the angle, length, and voice notes spelled out for each. The second part is a prompt pack — six real prompts you paste into the AI tool you already use, each with a "when to use" line and blanks you fill in.
The point is not more content for its own sake. It's getting the full return on work you already did, without letting a machine flatten how you sound or invent facts you'll have to walk back.

items: Solo operators and small teams who publish one good thing a week and want it to travel further.
Marketers tired of staring at a blank post when the source material is right there.
Founders and experts who write well but don't have time to reformat the same idea five ways by hand.
A one-source-to-many-assets map you can reuse every week.
A brand voice card you fill in once and paste into every prompt.
Six copy-paste prompts, each with a title and a "when to use" line.
A human-check step for every asset, so nothing goes out unverified or off-brand.
Pick your pillar. One substantial asset — a blog post, a recorded talk, a webinar. It needs enough substance to break into pieces.
Fill the voice card once. Describe how you sound. You'll paste it into every prompt so the drafts start in your register, not the tool's.
Extract the core ideas. Run prompt (a) to pull 3-5 ideas and the best quotable lines. Everything downstream builds on one idea at a time.
Generate the derivatives. Work down the map. Use prompts (b) through (e) for each format; use (f) whenever a draft sounds generic.
Human-check, then publish. Verify every claim and link, confirm nothing is fabricated or off-brand, and only then schedule.

blocks.text: This is the template. Part one is the map — start from a single pillar asset and fan it out. Part two is the six prompts.
Part 1 · One source → many assets

Start from one pillar (a blog post, talk, or webinar). Each row below is a derivative asset. The "Human check before publishing" column is not optional — it's the difference between fast and reckless.

cells.text: One idea, expanded, linking back to the pillar
Warm, direct, first person; sound like an email from you, not a press release
Confirm the pillar link works; verify any stat or claim; read the subject line aloud
Three angles from one idea: story, how-to, contrarian
Plain, specific, one idea per post; no hashtag soup
Check facts and any named people; make sure the three don't overlap; cut hype
Hook tweet, then the argument broken into beats
Short lines, one thought per tweet; the hook earns the scroll
Verify claims fit in context; confirm the last tweet links or CTAs correctly
Visual, punchy, one takeaway per slide; save the payoff for the last card
Check the claim on each slide; confirm the final CTA slide is accurate
One idea as a spoken hook + payoff
Conversational, spoken not written; say it out loud as you edit
Fact-check the hook (hooks tempt exaggeration); confirm the CTA
The question your pillar answers, stated plainly
Neutral, clear, no marketing spin; answer the question directly
Verify the answer is current and correct; link to the source doc
Where else this idea belongs (sales deck, onboarding, FAQ)
Plain and practical; for your team, not the public
Confirm you're not duplicating an existing internal asset

blocks.text: Notice the pattern: one idea from the pillar feeds several formats. You don't repurpose the whole post at once — you take one idea and dress it for each room.
Part 2 · The prompts
Fill the voice card once and paste it into every prompt where you see [brand voice]. Each prompt has its own Copy button. Replace anything in [brackets] before you run it.
Your brand voice card (fill once, paste everywhere)
When to use: Fill this in one time, then paste it into any prompt below that references [brand voice].

BRAND VOICE CARD Who we are: [one line — what you do and for whom] How we sound: [3-5 adjectives, e.g. warm, plain, direct, no hype] Words we use: [terms/phrases that sound like us] Words we avoid: [buzzwords, clichés, anything that sounds generic or AI-written] Reading level: [e.g. clear enough for a busy owner skimming on a phone] Point of view: [first person "I/we" or brand voice] One-line example of our voice: [paste a sentence you're proud of]
a) Extract the core ideas and quotable lines
When to use: First, right after you pick your pillar. Everything else builds on this.

Here is a pillar piece of content: [paste the blog post, transcript, or webinar notes]. Read it closely and give me: 1. The 3-5 core ideas, each as one plain sentence a reader would remember. 2. For each idea, the single best quotable line already in the text (exact words, no paraphrasing). 3. Any claim, number, or link in the piece that I should fact-check before I reuse it. Do not invent ideas or quotes that aren't in the source. If something is unclear, flag it instead of guessing.
b) Turn one idea into 3 LinkedIn posts
When to use: Once you've picked one idea from prompt (a) and want three distinct posts, not three versions of the same one.

[brand voice] Take this one idea: [paste one core idea and its quotable line]. Write 3 distinct LinkedIn posts from it, each a genuinely different angle: 1. A story — a short, specific moment that makes the point. 2. A how-to — a concrete, numbered or stepped takeaway. 3. A contrarian take — the common belief, then why it's wrong here. Rules: 120-220 words each. One idea per post. No hashtag walls, no "thrilled to announce," no filler. Sound like the voice card above. Keep any factual claim I can verify; if you're unsure of a fact, mark it [CHECK].
c) Write a newsletter section
When to use: When you want an email section that expands one idea and drives readers back to the pillar.

[brand voice] Write a newsletter section built around this idea: [paste one core idea]. It should link back to the full pillar here: [paste pillar URL]. Give me: - A subject line (under 55 characters). - Preview text (under 90 characters) that isn't a repeat of the subject. - A 200-350 word section that expands the idea, adds one concrete example, and ends with a clear link back to the pillar. Write it like an email from a person, not a broadcast. Keep any fact I can check; flag anything you're unsure of with [CHECK].
d) Draft a 30-60s short-video script
When to use: When you want a spoken script for a short reel or TikTok from one idea.

[brand voice] Write a 30-60 second short-form video script from this idea: [paste one core idea]. Structure: - HOOK (first 3 seconds): one line that earns the next 5 seconds. No clickbait, no exaggeration I can't back up. - 3 BEATS: three short spoken points that build the idea. - CTA: one clear next step (watch the full piece, comment, follow). Write it to be spoken, not read — short sentences, natural rhythm, ~90-150 words total. Mark any factual claim I should verify with [CHECK].
e) Repurpose into an X / Twitter thread
When to use: When one idea deserves a threaded argument rather than a single post.

[brand voice] Turn this idea into an X/Twitter thread: [paste one core idea and its quotable line]. Give me: - 1 hook tweet that makes someone stop scrolling (no "a thread 🧵" cliché unless it truly fits). - 5-7 follow-on tweets, one thought each, that build the argument. - A final tweet with a clear CTA or link back to the pillar: [paste pillar URL]. Keep each tweet under 280 characters. Short lines. No hype words. Flag any claim I should verify with [CHECK].
f) Adapt tone and fix generic drafts
When to use: Any time a draft reads flat, generic, or obviously machine-written.

[brand voice: warm, plain, no hype] Here is a draft: [paste the draft]. Rewrite it to match the brand voice card above. Specifically: - Cut anything that sounds generic, corporate, or AI-written (empty openers, "in today's fast-paced world," "unlock," "seamless," "game-changer," "leverage," "delve"). - Keep every fact and link exactly as written — do not add claims or numbers that weren't there. - Prefer plain words and short sentences. Say the real thing. Then list, in one or two lines, what you changed and why — so I can spot patterns and edit the next draft myself.
A note on the human check

Every asset in the map has a human-check column for a reason. Before anything publishes: fact-check the claims, verify the links actually go where they should, and confirm nothing is fabricated or off-brand. AI is happy to invent a statistic or a quote that reads perfectly and never existed. The person hitting publish owns what it says — not the tool.

Before you publish: AI-repurposed content can drift from the facts, invent statistics or quotes, or flatten your voice into something generic. A human verifies every claim and link, every time, before it goes out. Don't republish someone else's content as your own — repurpose only what you made or have the right to use. This is general education, not legal advice; check your own obligations before you publish.

title: Meeting Summary Prompt Pack
summary: Copy-paste prompts that turn a meeting transcript into a summary, decision log, and owned action items while exposing missing names, dates, and ambiguities.
audience: Teams creating accountable records and follow-up from authorized meeting transcripts.
methodology: Mark missing information instead of guessing
assumptions: The transcript was lawfully and appropriately created
limitations: Transcripts can misidentify speakers or omit context
Recording, consent, confidentiality, and retention duties vary
editorialIntro: A transcript is not a summary. These eight copy-paste prompts take the raw, rambling record of a meeting and hand back the parts that matter: a clean recap, a decision log, and action items with a named owner and a due date — and nothing the room never actually said.

blocks.text: Eight prompts you paste into whatever AI tool you already use, each doing one job in the flow from raw transcript to shared follow-up. Start with the master summary, then reach for the extractors, the email draft, or the privacy pass depending on what you need. Every prompt carries the same rule: work only from what's in the transcript, and flag anything unclear instead of filling the gap with a plausible guess.

You bring the transcript — from your notetaker, your recorder's auto-caption, or notes you typed live. The prompts bring the structure. The one thing they can't bring is a human who confirms the owners actually agreed to their tasks. That part stays yours.

items: Whoever got stuck writing up the meeting: the organizer, the chief-of-staff, the person who happened to hit record.
Managers who run a lot of standing meetings and want the recap out the door in minutes, not the next morning.
Teams tired of the "wait, who was doing that?" message three days after every call.
A master summary prompt that produces a TL;DR, decisions, action items, open questions, and risks in one pass.
Focused extractors for action items, decisions, chase lists, and a leadership-ready one-paragraph version.
A follow-up email draft prompt and a gap-finder that tells you exactly what the transcript left ambiguous.
A redaction pass to catch anything sensitive before you hit send, plus a short worked example so you can see the shape of good output.
Get a transcript. Any format works — timestamps and speaker labels help, but plain text is fine. Clean up obvious garble if you can; you don't have to.
Run the master summary first. Paste your transcript where each prompt says [paste transcript here], and read what comes back before you trust it.
Reach for a focused prompt when you need one. Want just the action items as a table? Just the decisions? Just an email? Grab the matching prompt below.
Run the gap-finder, then verify. It surfaces every missing name, date, or owner. Fill those in yourself, and confirm each owner actually agreed before you assign them anything.
Do a privacy pass before sharing widely. Especially if the meeting touched money, people, or anything under NDA.

blocks.text: Eight prompts, each in its own box with its own Copy button. Replace the [bracketed] placeholders with your own text. They are written to be strict about invention on purpose — an AI would rather give you a tidy, confident answer than an honest "the transcript doesn't say," so each prompt pushes hard in the other direction.
1. Master summary
When to use: your first pass on any transcript — the one prompt that gives you the whole picture.

You are summarizing a meeting from its transcript. Use ONLY what appears in the transcript below. Do not add, infer, or smooth over anything. If a detail (a name, a date, an owner, a decision) is missing or unclear, write [UNCLEAR] in its place rather than guessing. Produce the summary in exactly these sections: TL;DR - Three bullets, one line each, capturing what this meeting was actually about and what changed as a result. DECISIONS MADE - List each concrete decision the group reached. If nothing was decided, write "No decisions recorded." ACTION ITEMS - One line each, formatted: Owner — Task — Due date - If the owner or due date was never stated, write [UNCLEAR] in that slot. OPEN QUESTIONS - Anything raised but not resolved. RISKS / FLAGS - Concerns, blockers, or dependencies mentioned. If none, write "None raised." Transcript: [paste transcript here]
2. Action items as a table
When to use: you only need the "who does what by when," and you want it clean enough to paste into a doc or tracker.

From the transcript below, extract every action item — a task someone committed to or was assigned. Use only what the transcript states. Return a table with these columns: Owner | Task | Due | Source quote - Owner: the person responsible. If never named, write [UNCLEAR]. - Task: the specific thing to do, in a few words. - Due: the stated deadline. If none was given, write [UNCLEAR]. - Source quote: the short line from the transcript where this was said, so I can verify it. Do not invent tasks that were only vaguely gestured at. If someone said "we should probably look into that" with no owner, list it with [UNCLEAR] owners rather than skipping or assigning it. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
3. Decision log
When to use: you need a record of what was actually decided and why — for the wiki, the board update, or your own memory.

From the transcript below, build a decision log. A decision is a choice the group actually settled on — not a topic discussed, not an option floated and dropped. Return a table with these columns: Decision | Rationale | Who decided | Date - Rationale: the reason given in the meeting, if any. If none was stated, write [UNCLEAR]. - Who decided: the person or group who made the call. If unclear, write [UNCLEAR]. - Date: use the meeting date if that's the only date available: [meeting date]. If a discussion ended without a clear decision, do not manufacture one. It's fine to return only the decisions that were genuinely made. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
4. Follow-up email to attendees
When to use: right after the meeting, when you want to send everyone a recap that reminds each person of their own commitments.

Draft a short, professional follow-up email to the people who attended this meeting. Base it only on the transcript below — do not add commitments or details that weren't discussed. The email should: - Open with one or two sentences on what the meeting covered and any key decisions. - List action items grouped so each attendee can find their own, in the form "Name — task — due date." - Where an owner or date is missing, write [UNCLEAR] so I can fill it in before sending, rather than you guessing. - Close with a brief, friendly line inviting corrections. Keep it concise and warm — the tone of a helpful colleague, not a legal memo. Sign it from [your name]. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
5. "Who owns what" chase list
When to use: you're the organizer and need a person-by-person view of who you're waiting on.

From the transcript below, build a chase list for the meeting organizer, grouped by person. For each person who took on any commitment, list their name as a heading, then their tasks beneath it with due dates. Format: [Person's name] - Task — Due date - Task — Due date Rules: - Use only what the transcript states. Missing owner or date → [UNCLEAR]. - Add a final group titled "UNASSIGNED" for any task with no clear owner, so nothing falls through the cracks. - Do not assign a task to someone unless the transcript shows they accepted it. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
6. Ambiguity & gap finder
When to use: before you trust any summary — this tells you exactly what a human needs to fill in.

Read the transcript below and act as a careful editor whose only job is to find gaps. Do NOT summarize. Do NOT fix anything. Just list every place where a name, a date, an owner, or a decision is missing, vague, or ambiguous, so a human can resolve it. For each gap, give: - What's unclear (e.g., "owner of the pricing task") - The nearby transcript line where it comes up - What question a human should ask to resolve it Be thorough — it's better to flag a borderline case than to let a wrong assumption slip into the summary. If the transcript is actually clear and complete, say so plainly. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
7. Executive one-paragraph version
When to use: a leader who wasn't in the room needs the gist in fifteen seconds.

Write a single paragraph — no more than five sentences — summarizing this meeting for [leader's name/role], who was not present and has limited time. Cover: what the meeting was about, the most important decision or outcome, and anything that needs their attention or approval. Use plain language, no jargon, no bullet points. Base it only on the transcript below. If something a leader would want to know is genuinely unclear from the transcript, say so in the paragraph rather than inventing it. Transcript: [paste transcript here]
8. Redaction & privacy pass
When to use: right before you share the summary beyond the people who were in the room.

Review the meeting summary or transcript below and act as a privacy reviewer. Your job is to flag — not remove — anything that probably should not leave the room before it's shared more widely. Flag and list: - Named individuals whose identity may be sensitive in this context (personnel issues, performance, health, legal). - Financial figures, pricing, salaries, or commercial terms. - Anything that sounds confidential, under NDA, or legally sensitive. - Off-the-record asides or "don't repeat this" moments. For each flag, quote the relevant line and suggest whether to remove it, generalize it, or keep it only for a smaller audience. Do not rewrite the document — just give me the list so I can decide. Content to review: [paste transcript or summary here]
See the shape of good output
Here is a short raw transcript snippet and the clean action-item table it should turn into — so you know what "good" looks like before you run your own.
Raw transcript snippet

[00:12] Priya: I'll get the revised budget over to finance by Friday. [00:14] Marcus: Good. And someone needs to loop in legal on the vendor contract. [00:15] Priya: Dana, can you take that? Maybe by end of next week? [00:15] Dana: Yep, I'll reach out to legal — end of next week works.

cells.text: "I'll get the revised budget over to finance by Friday."
Loop in legal on the vendor contract
"I'll reach out to legal — end of next week works."

blocks.text: Notice what the table did not do: it didn't turn Marcus's "someone needs to loop in legal" into an action item on its own, because that line had no owner — Dana only became the owner once she accepted. That's the difference between reading the transcript and inventing from it.

Before you send anything out: AI models invent owners, dates, and even whole decisions that were never said — confidently and in clean formatting, which makes the invention easy to miss. Always read the summary against the transcript, and confirm each owner actually agreed to their task before you assign it. Don't paste confidential transcripts — anything with client names, financials, personnel matters, or NDA'd material — into consumer AI tiers where your text may be used for training; use a private or approved tool for those. This is general education, not legal advice; check your own obligations before you move sensitive material anywhere.

title: SOP Prompt Pack
summary: Ten copy-paste prompts that turn a process in someone's head into a clear, testable standard operating procedure with uncertainty and human review built in.
audience: Owners, managers, operations leads, and teams documenting repeatable processes.
methodology: Ask one question at a time
assumptions: A knowledgeable human completes and validates the prompts
The resulting SOP is tested before adoption
limitations: Prompts cannot recover undisclosed tacit knowledge
High-stakes procedures require qualified legal, safety, financial, privacy, or regulatory review
editorialIntro: Your best process usually lives in one person's head, and it walks out the door with them. These ten prompts draw it out one question at a time and shape it into a procedure a new hire could actually follow — with a human checking the work at every step that matters.

blocks.text: Ten prompts, run in order, that walk an AI tool through building a real SOP with you. The first interviews you to get the process out of your head. The rest draft it, test it against a first-day hire, add the "if this, then that" branches, insert quality checks, plain out the language, and set a plan that keeps it from going stale. You bring the knowledge; the prompts bring the structure and the patience to ask again when your answer is fuzzy.

None of this replaces your judgment. The pack keeps a person in the loop at every turn — you approve each step, and the prompts are written to flag what they don't know rather than paper over it with a confident guess.

items: Owners and managers tired of answering the same "how do I do this again?" and ready to write it down once.
Anyone onboarding a new hire into a job only one person currently knows how to do.
Operations and support leads who need repeatable, auditable procedures instead of tribal knowledge.
Small teams with no technical writer who still need documentation people will actually open.
Ten copy-paste prompts, each with a short title and a one-line note on when to use it.
A full workflow: interview, draft, stress-test, add logic, add checks, simplify, checklist, flag risk, onboarding version, maintenance plan.
Bracketed placeholders you fill with your own process, tools, and role names.
Built-in [NEEDS INPUT] markers so the AI names what it doesn't know instead of inventing it.

blocks.text: Run the prompts in order, in the same chat, so the AI carries the context from each step into the next. Fill in every [bracketed placeholder] before you send — the more specific you are, the sharper the SOP. Start with prompt 1 and let the interview finish; resist jumping to the draft before the tool actually understands your process.

One rule never bends: never publish a high-stakes SOP without a qualified human approving it. Anything touching money, safety, health, legal exposure, or someone's employment gets a real expert's sign-off before it goes live. The AI is your fast first draft, not your final authority.
Ten prompts, in the order you'd run them. Copy one, fill in the brackets, send it, then move to the next.
1. Interview me to extract the process
When to use it: first, before anything is written — to get the process out of your head.

You are helping me write a standard operating procedure (SOP) for a task I know how to do but have never documented. The task is: [DESCRIBE THE TASK IN ONE SENTENCE]. Interview me to pull out everything a new person would need. Ask ONE question at a time and wait for my answer before asking the next — do not batch questions or move on until my answer is clear. Cover, in roughly this order: - What triggers this task? (an event, a schedule, a request from someone) - What tools, systems, logins, or access does someone need before they can start? - The exact ordered steps, from the very first action to the last. - Decision points: places where the right next step depends on something ("if the order is over $500, then…"). - Exceptions and edge cases: what goes wrong, and what someone does when it does. - Definition of done: how does a person know the task is finished and correct? If one of my answers is vague, ask a follow-up before moving on. When you believe you have enough to write a complete SOP, say so and give me a short bulleted summary of what you captured so I can confirm or correct it before we draft anything.
2. Draft the SOP from my answers
When to use it: once the interview is done and you've confirmed the summary.

Using only what I told you in the interview, draft a complete SOP for [TASK NAME]. Do not invent steps, tools, or details I didn't give you. Structure it exactly like this: - Purpose — one or two sentences on why this task matters. - When to run — the trigger(s) that start it. - Owner — the role responsible (use [NEEDS INPUT] if I didn't say). - Prerequisites — access, tools, and information needed before starting. - Steps — numbered, in order, one clear action per step. - Decision points — any "if X, then Y" branches, called out clearly. - Common mistakes — errors people make and how to avoid them. Wherever you're missing information or would have to guess, write [NEEDS INPUT] in that spot instead of filling it with a plausible guess. At the end, list every [NEEDS INPUT] marker as a short checklist of questions for me to answer.
3. Beginner stress-test
When to use it: after you have a draft, to find what a brand-new person couldn't follow.

Read the SOP below as if you are a brand-new hire on your first day. You know nothing about our company, our tools, or our shorthand — only what's written on the page. Go through it and flag: - Every step that assumes knowledge a beginner wouldn't have ("log into the portal" — which portal? where?). - Every undefined term, acronym, internal name, or piece of jargon. - Every instruction that could reasonably be done more than one way (ambiguous wording). - Any point where you'd have to stop and ask a coworker to keep going. For each item, quote the exact line, say what's unclear, and suggest what it should say instead. Don't rewrite the whole SOP — just give me the list of gaps so I can fix them. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
4. Add decision branches and "if X then Y" logic
When to use it: when the real task isn't a straight line — it forks based on conditions.

The SOP below is written as a single straight-line sequence, but the real task branches depending on conditions. Help me add that logic. Based on what I've told you (and asking me where you're unsure), identify every point where the next step depends on something — the amount, the customer type, the answer to a question, whether something passed or failed. For each one, write it as an explicit branch: IF [condition], THEN [do this] → go to step [X] ELSE [do this instead] → go to step [Y] Keep the branches easy to scan. Where you think a branch probably exists but I haven't told you the exact rule, mark it [NEEDS INPUT: what's the threshold / rule here?] rather than guessing a number or policy. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
5. Insert quality checkpoints and verification steps
When to use it: before publishing, to catch errors at the risky points.

Go through the SOP below and find every step where a mistake would be costly, hard to undo, or invisible until later — sending money, deleting data, publishing something public, changing a customer's account, anything irreversible. For each of those risky steps, add: - A quality checkpoint: a specific thing to confirm BEFORE doing the action ("Confirm the account number matches the invoice before submitting"). - A verification step: a specific way to confirm AFTER the action that it worked correctly ("Refresh the record and confirm the status now reads 'Paid'"). Write these so they're concrete and checkable, not vague ("double-check everything" is not acceptable — say exactly what to check and how). Insert them inline at the right spot and show me the updated SOP with the new checks marked so I can see what you added. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
6. Rewrite in plain language
When to use it: when the SOP is accurate but reads stiff, dense, or over-worded.

Rewrite the SOP below in plain, direct language aimed at about an 8th-grade reading level — the kind of writing anyone on the team could follow on a busy day. Rules: - Keep every step, decision branch, and check exactly as-is in meaning. Do not drop, merge, or reorder anything, and do not change any number, name, threshold, or rule. - Use short sentences and everyday words. Cut filler. Prefer "click Save" over "proceed to initiate the save operation." - Start each step with a clear verb. - Keep any required technical terms, but add a plain-language explanation the first time each one appears. If simplifying a step would risk changing what it actually means, leave that step's wording alone and flag it with [KEPT AS-IS: simplifying might change the meaning]. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
7. Generate a one-page quick-reference checklist
When to use it: for the person who already knows the SOP and just needs a reminder.

Turn the SOP below into a one-page quick-reference checklist for someone who has already been trained and just needs a reminder while they work. Make it: - Short enough to fit on a single page. - A scannable checklist with a checkbox for each key action. - Written as brief action lines, not full paragraphs. - Inclusive of the critical decision points (as short "if… then…" lines) and the must-do verification checks, so nothing important gets skipped. Do not add anything that isn't in the full SOP. At the top, note the SOP name and "Full version required for training." Keep it tight — this is a reminder card, not the manual. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
8. Flag steps that need expert sign-off
When to use it: before publishing anything that could carry legal, safety, or compliance weight.

Review the SOP below and flag any step that carries legal, safety, financial, privacy, or regulatory/compliance weight — anything where getting it wrong could harm someone, break a law or regulation, void a contract, or expose the company. For each flagged step: - Quote the exact step. - Name why it needs expert review (e.g., "handles customer payment data," "makes a hiring/termination decision," "involves a safety procedure"). - Say what KIND of expert should sign off (lawyer, accountant, safety officer, HR, compliance). Do NOT tell me what the correct legal, safety, or compliance answer is, and do not rewrite these steps to "make them compliant." You are only flagging where a qualified human must review before this SOP goes live. If nothing needs expert sign-off, say so plainly. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
9. Create an onboarding version
When to use it: when you're training someone new and want a teachable, walk-through version.

Turn the SOP below into an onboarding version for someone doing this task for the very first time. Assume they need more context and hand-holding than the standard SOP gives. For each step: - Add a short "why this matters" note where the reason isn't obvious, so the trainee understands, not just memorizes. - Where a screenshot would help someone find a button, menu, or screen, insert a marker: [SCREENSHOT NEEDED: what it should show]. - The first time each tool or system is mentioned, add a "Where to find it" note: how to open it, the URL or app name, and who to ask for access. Use [NEEDS INPUT: where is this / who grants access?] if I haven't told you. Keep all the original steps, checks, and decision branches intact. The goal is a version a new hire could learn from with a trainer beside them. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]
10. Set a maintenance plan
When to use it: last — so the SOP stays true after the process changes.

Write a short maintenance plan to keep the SOP below accurate over time. Base the owner and details on what I've told you, and use [NEEDS INPUT] where you don't have the information. Include: - Owner — the role (not a person's name) responsible for keeping this SOP current. - Review date — a recommended review cadence (e.g., every 6 months) and the next review date to put on the calendar. - Change log format — a simple table format for recording edits: date, what changed, who changed it, why. - Staleness signals — a short checklist of signs the SOP is out of date: a tool changed its interface, a step now points to a system we no longer use, people are quietly doing it differently than written, a decision threshold changed, or the last review date has passed. Format this as a "Maintenance" section I can paste at the end of the SOP. SOP: [PASTE THE CURRENT SOP HERE]

Read this before you publish anything: AI writes confidently even when it's wrong — it will happily invent a plausible-but-incorrect step, threshold, or tool name to fill a gap. That's exactly why these prompts use [NEEDS INPUT] markers: keep them in, and answer every one against reality instead of letting the model guess. Verify each step by actually doing the task or watching someone who knows it. Any SOP touching compliance, safety, money, health, or employment needs a qualified human's sign-off before it goes live (that's what prompt 8 is for). This is general education, not legal, medical, or financial advice.

editorialSections.title: Want your whole SOP library built with you?

blocks.text: We'll sit down with your team, run these prompts on your real processes, and leave you with a core set of SOPs your people will actually follow — reviewed, plain-spoken, and ready to hand a new hire. Bring the process; we'll bring the questions.
